title: Differentiation trig
unit: IAL Pure Mathematics (P3) - unit inferred from file name

questions.question: Given x = 6 sin^2(2y), 0 < y < pi/4, show that dy/dx = 1/(A sqrt(Bx - x^2)) where A and B are integers to be found.
questions.answer: A = 4, B = 6, so dy/dx = 1/(4 sqrt(6x - x^2))
steps: Differentiate: dx/dy = 6 x 2 sin(2y) x cos(2y) x 2 = 24 sin(2y)cos(2y) = 12 sin(4y).
From x = 6 sin^2(2y): sin(2y) = sqrt(x/6), since 0 < 2y < pi/2 so sin and cos are positive.
cos(2y) = sqrt(1 - x/6).
sin(4y) = 2 sin(2y)cos(2y) = 2 sqrt(x(6 - x))/6 = sqrt(6x - x^2)/3.
So dx/dy = 12 x sqrt(6x - x^2)/3 = 4 sqrt(6x - x^2).
dy/dx = 1/(4 sqrt(6x - x^2)), so A = 4 and B = 6.

questions.question: A curve C has equation y = f(x) = arcsin(x/2), -2 <= x <= 2, -pi/2 <= y <= pi/2. Sketch C.
questions.answer: Increasing S-shaped curve from (-2, -pi/2) through the origin to (2, pi/2)
steps: Domain -2 <= x <= 2 and range -pi/2 <= y <= pi/2 set the ends of the curve.
At x = -2: y = arcsin(-1) = -pi/2; at x = 0: y = 0; at x = 2: y = arcsin(1) = pi/2.
arcsin is increasing, so the curve rises steadily from (-2, -pi/2) through (0, 0) to (2, pi/2).
The curve is symmetric about the origin (odd function).

questions.question: Given x = 2 sin y, show that dy/dx = 1/sqrt(A - x^2), where A is a constant to be found, for the curve y = arcsin(x/2).
steps: Differentiate x = 2 sin y: dx/dy = 2 cos y.
So dy/dx = 1/(2 cos y).
cos y = sqrt(1 - sin^2 y) = sqrt(1 - x^2/4), since cos y >= 0 for -pi/2 <= y <= pi/2.
2 cos y = 2 sqrt(1 - x^2/4) = sqrt(4 - x^2).
So dy/dx = 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) and A = 4.

questions.question: The point P lies on C and has y coordinate pi/4. Find the equation of the tangent to C at P, in the form y = mx + c, where m and c are constants to be found.
steps: At P, y = pi/4, so x = 2 sin(pi/4) = sqrt(2). P = (sqrt(2), pi/4).
Gradient: dy/dx = 1/sqrt(4 - x^2) = 1/sqrt(4 - 2) = 1/sqrt(2).
Tangent: y - pi/4 = (1/sqrt(2))(x - sqrt(2)).
Expand: y = x/sqrt(2) - 1 + pi/4.
So m = sqrt(2)/2 and c = pi/4 - 1.

questions.question: P has (x, y) coordinates (p, pi/2) and lies on the curve x = (4y - sin 2y)^2. Find the exact value of p.
steps: Substitute y = pi/2: 4y = 2 pi and sin(2y) = sin(pi) = 0.
So p = 4 pi^2.

questions.question: The point P with coordinates (4 pi^2, pi/2) lies on the curve x = (4y - sin 2y)^2. The tangent to the curve at P cuts the y-axis at the point A. Use calculus to find the coordinates of A.
steps: dx/dy = 2(4y - sin 2y)(4 - 2 cos 2y), using the chain rule.
At y = pi/2: 4y - sin 2y = 2 pi and 4 - 2 cos(pi) = 6.
dx/dy = 2 x 2 pi x 6 = 24 pi, so dy/dx = 1/(24 pi).
Tangent at P: y - pi/2 = (x - 4 pi^2)/(24 pi).
On the y-axis x = 0: y = pi/2 - 4 pi^2/(24 pi) = pi/2 - pi/6 = pi/3.

questions.question: f(x) = (2x + 5)^2/(x - 3), x not equal to 3. (a) Find f'(x) in the form P(x)/Q(x), where P(x) and Q(x) are fully factorised quadratic expressions. (b) Hence find the range of values of x for which f(x) is increasing.
steps: f is increasing when f'(x) > 0. The denominator is always positive for x not equal to 3.
Critical values are x = -5/2 and x = 17/2; the quadratic (2x + 5)(2x - 17) is positive outside these roots.
So f is increasing for x < -5/2 or x > 17/2.

questions.question: g(x) = x sqrt(sin 4x), 0 <= x < pi/4. The curve y = g(x) has a maximum point M. Show that the x coordinate of M satisfies tan(4x) + kx = 0, where k is a constant to be found.
steps: Write g(x) = x(sin 4x)^(1/2).
Product rule: g'(x) = (sin 4x)^(1/2) + x(1/2)(sin 4x)^(-1/2)(4 cos 4x).
Simplify: g'(x) = sqrt(sin 4x) + 2x cos(4x)/sqrt(sin 4x).
Set g'(x) = 0 and multiply by sqrt(sin 4x) > 0: sin 4x + 2x cos 4x = 0.
Divide by cos 4x: tan 4x + 2x = 0, so k = 2.

questions.question: The curve C has equation y = g(x) where g(x) = e^(3x) sec(2x), -pi/4 < x < pi/4. Find g'(x).
steps: Product rule: g'(x) = 3e^(3x) sec(2x) + e^(3x) d/dx[sec(2x)].
d/dx[sec(2x)] = 2 sec(2x) tan(2x).
So g'(x) = 3e^(3x) sec(2x) + 2e^(3x) sec(2x) tan(2x).
Factor: g'(x) = e^(3x) sec(2x)(3 + 2 tan(2x)).

questions.question: For the curve y = e^(3x) sec(2x), -pi/4 < x < pi/4, find the x coordinate of the stationary point of C.
steps: From part (a), g'(x) = 0 requires 3 + 2 tan(2x) = 0, since e^(3x) and sec(2x) are never zero.
Within -pi/4 < x < pi/4, we have -pi/2 < 2x < pi/2, so 2x = arctan(-3/2).

questions.question: A different curve has equation x = ln(sin y), 0 < y < pi/2. Show that dy/dx = e^x/f(x), where f(x) is a function of e^x to be found.
questions.answer: f(x) = sqrt(1 - e^(2x)), so dy/dx = e^x/sqrt(1 - e^(2x))
steps: Differentiate x = ln(sin y): dx/dy = cos y/sin y = cot y.
So dy/dx = 1/cot y = tan y.
From x = ln(sin y), sin y = e^x.
cos y = sqrt(1 - sin^2 y) = sqrt(1 - e^(2x)), since cos y > 0 for 0 < y < pi/2.
tan y = sin y/cos y = e^x/sqrt(1 - e^(2x)), so f(x) = sqrt(1 - e^(2x)).

questions.question: f(x) = x cos(x/3), x > 0. Find f'(x).
steps: Product rule: f'(x) = 1 x cos(x/3) + x x d/dx[cos(x/3)].
So f'(x) = cos(x/3) - (x/3) sin(x/3).

questions.question: f(x) = x cos(x/3), x > 0. Show that f'(x) = 0 can be written as x = k arctan(k/x), where k is an integer to be found.
steps: Set f'(x) = 0: cos(x/3) = (x/3) sin(x/3).
Divide by cos(x/3) (non-zero at the root): 1 = (x/3) tan(x/3).
So tan(x/3) = 3/x.
Take arctan: x/3 = arctan(3/x), so x = 3 arctan(3/x).
So k = 3.

questions.question: Starting with x1 = 2.5, use the iteration x(n+1) = 3 arctan(3/xn) to calculate x2 and x6, giving answers to 3 decimal places.
steps: x6 = 3 arctan(3/2.572) = 2.586 to 3 decimal places.

questions.question: Using a suitable interval and a suitable function that should be stated, show that a root of f'(x) = 0 is 2.581 correct to 3 decimal places.
questions.answer: Use h(x) = x - 3 arctan(3/x); h(2.5805) < 0 and h(2.5815) > 0, so the root is 2.581 to 3 d.p.
steps: From part (b), f'(x) = 0 is equivalent to h(x) = x - 3 arctan(3/x) = 0 (for x > 0).
There is a sign change in [2.5805, 2.5815] and h is continuous, so a root lies there.
Therefore the root is 2.581 correct to 3 decimal places.

keywords: a over x squared plus b
questions.question: The curve C has equation x = 3 tan(y - pi/6), x in R, -pi/3 < y < 2pi/3. Show that dy/dx = a/(x^2 + b), where a and b are integers to be found.
steps: Let theta = y - pi/6, so x = 3 tan(theta).
dx/dtheta = 3 sec^2(theta), so dy/dx = 1/(3 sec^2(theta)) = cos^2(theta)/3.
Use cos^2(theta) = 1/(1 + tan^2(theta)) with tan(theta) = x/3.

questions.question: The point P with y coordinate pi/3 lies on the curve C where x = 3 tan(y - pi/6). The tangent to C at P crosses the x-axis at the point Q. Find, in simplest form, the exact x coordinate of Q.
steps: At P, y = pi/3, so x = 3 tan(pi/6) = 3/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3).
Gradient at P: dy/dx = 3/(x^2 + 9) = 3/(3 + 9) = 1/4.
Tangent: y - pi/3 = (1/4)(x - sqrt(3)).
On the x-axis, y = 0: -pi/3 = (1/4)(x - sqrt(3)).
x - sqrt(3) = -4pi/3, so x = sqrt(3) - 4pi/3.

questions.question: Figure 5 shows the curve with equation y = (1 + 2cos x)/(1 + sin x), -pi/2 < x < 3pi/2. The point M is the minimum point on the curve. Show that the x coordinate of M is a solution of 2 sin x + cos x = -2.
questions.answer: Shown: 2 sin x + cos x = -2 at the minimum
steps: Quotient rule: dy/dx = [(-2 sin x)(1 + sin x) - (1 + 2 cos x)(cos x)]/(1 + sin x)^2.
Expand numerator: -2 sin x - 2 sin^2 x - cos x - 2 cos^2 x.
Use sin^2 x + cos^2 x = 1: numerator = -2 sin x - cos x - 2.
So dy/dx = -(2 sin x + cos x + 2)/(1 + sin x)^2.
At the minimum dy/dx = 0, so 2 sin x + cos x + 2 = 0, i.e. 2 sin x + cos x = -2.

questions.question: Hence find, to 3 significant figures, the x coordinate of M, the minimum point on y = (1 + 2 cos x)/(1 + sin x), -pi/2 < x < 3pi/2.
steps: Let s = sin x. From 2 sin x + cos x = -2: cos x = -2 - 2s.
s = -1 gives x = -pi/2 or 3pi/2, which are excluded by the domain.
s = -3/5 gives cos x = -4/5, so x = pi + arctan(3/4) approx 3.7851.
To 3 significant figures, x = 3.79.

questions.question: The curve has equation y = 2 cos(3x) - 3x + 4, x > 0. The curve crosses the x-axis at P with x coordinate alpha. Show that alpha lies between 0.8 and 0.9.
questions.answer: g(0.8) = 0.125 > 0 and g(0.9) = -0.508 < 0, so alpha lies between 0.8 and 0.9
steps: Let g(x) = 2 cos(3x) - 3x + 4, which is continuous.
There is a sign change on [0.8, 0.9], so alpha lies between 0.8 and 0.9.

questions.question: The iteration x(n+1) = (1/3) arccos(1.5x_n - 2) can be used to find alpha. Using this iteration with x1 = 0.8, find to 4 decimal places (i) x2 and (ii) x5.
steps: So x2 = 0.8327 and x5 = 0.8110 to 4 decimal places.

questions.question: Q and R are local minimum points on y = 2 cos(3x) - 3x + 4, x > 0, with x coordinates beta and lambda, the two smallest values of x at which local minima occur. Using calculus, find the exact values of beta and lambda.
steps: dy/dx = -6 sin(3x) - 3, so stationary points satisfy sin(3x) = -1/2.
d^2y/dx^2 = -18 cos(3x); a minimum needs d^2y/dx^2 > 0, so cos(3x) < 0.
The solutions of sin(3x) = -1/2 with 3x > 0 are 3x = 7pi/6, 11pi/6, 19pi/6, ...
At 3x = 7pi/6, cos(3x) = -sqrt(3)/2 < 0, so this is a minimum; at 11pi/6 cos > 0, so it is a maximum.
The next minimum is at 3x = 19pi/6, giving x = 19pi/18.
So beta = 7pi/18 and lambda = 19pi/18.

questions.question: The curve C has equation y = x^2 cos(x/2), 0 < x <= pi. The curve has a stationary point at P. Show, using calculus, that the x coordinate of P is a solution of x = 2 arctan(4/x).
questions.answer: Shown: at P, tan(x/2) = 4/x, so x = 2 arctan(4/x)
steps: Product rule: dy/dx = 2x cos(x/2) - (x^2/2) sin(x/2).
Set dy/dx = 0 and divide by x (x > 0): 2 cos(x/2) = (x/2) sin(x/2).
Divide by cos(x/2): 2 = (x/2) tan(x/2), so tan(x/2) = 4/x.
Take arctan: x/2 = arctan(4/x), so x = 2 arctan(4/x).

questions.question: Using the iteration x(n+1) = 2 arctan(4/xn) with x1 = 2, find the values of x2 and x6, giving answers to 3 decimal places.
steps: x6 = 2 arctan(4/2.1502) = 2.155 to 3 decimal places.

questions.question: Figure 4 shows a sketch of the curve with equation x = (2y^2 + 6)/(3y - 3). Find dx/dy, giving your answer as a fully simplified fraction.
steps: Write x = u/v with u = 2y^2 + 6 and v = 3y - 3.
Quotient rule with respect to y: dx/dy = (v du/dy - u dv/dy)/v^2.
du/dy = 4y and dv/dy = 3.
Denominator = (3y - 3)^2 = 9(y - 1)^2.

questions.question: The tangents at points P and Q on the curve x = (2y^2 + 6)/(3y - 3) are parallel to the y-axis, as shown in Figure 4. Use the answer to part (a) to find the equations of these two tangents.
steps: A tangent parallel to the y-axis has dx/dy = 0.
At y = 3: x = (18 + 6)/(9 - 3) = 4, so tangent x = 4 (point Q).
These match Figure 4: P is left of the origin and Q is to the right.
